prompt: Consider the view that all thinking is a bodily process like perceiving, as the ancients held, and evaluate whether Aristotle's critique of this view depends on his theory of phantasia.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis The ancient materialist tradition, as Aristotle reports in *De Anima* III.3, maintained that all thinking is a bodily process fundamentally akin to perceiving—that the soul knows like by like, and that cognition is therefore exhaustively reducible to the physical affection of sense (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 47–48). Against this thoroughgoing assimilation of νοεῖν to αἰσθάνεσθαι, Aristotle develops a sustained critique whose force depends, in decisive ways, upon his theory of φαντασία. For if thinking were simply identical with perceiving, then there would be no faculty capable of mediating between the immediacy of sensory contact and the generality of thought; yet Aristotle insists that "to the thinking soul images serve as if they were contents of perception (and when it asserts or denies them to be good or bad it avoids or pursues them)" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, pp. 47–48). This crucial passage reveals that the thinking soul does not operate upon percepts directly but upon φαντάσματα—images that function as quasi-perceptual contents without requiring the present activity of the external sense organ. Accordingly, phantasia occupies a structural position that contrasts with aisthesis even as it depends upon it: perception must have occurred for phantasia to generate its images, yet phantasia persists and operates in the absence of the perceived object, thereby opening a domain of cognitive activity irreducible to bodily affection alone. As Victor Caston argues, "the thesis must maintain only that thinking consists in the same kind of process as perceiving, not strict identity," and it is precisely phantasia that reveals the inadequacy of even this weakened materialist claim, since the image-making faculty introduces the possibility of error and falsehood where perception of proper sensibles remains largely veridical (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4). The internal distinctions within phantasia—between its lower, sensory grade, shared with non-rational animals, and its higher, deliberative grade, operative in rational agents—will be explored in subsequent sections; here it suffices the very existence of phantasia as a capacity distinct from perception already undermines the ancient equation of thinking with bodily process. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The φάντασμα, as the product or correlate of φαντασία, constitutes the indispensable medium through which the soul engages objects no longer present to sense. That the phantasma depends upon phantasia as its generative source is evident from the fact that, without the prior exercise of the image-making capacity, there would be no residual sensory content available for thought to take up and deploy. Aristotle's account in *De Anima* III.7 speaks of calculation about the future "as though it involved a kind of picturing," where one reasons "using the phantasmata or noëmata in the soul, as if one saw the things, and plans for the future in view of the present" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). Martha Nussbaum the inclusion of noëmata alongside phantasmata in this passage "indicates that Aristotle is not committing himself" to a reductive identification of all thought-content with sensory pictures (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). Indeed, the phantasma possesses a dual nature—a tension acknowledged in the corpus—for it can serve simultaneously as an object of contemplation in its own right (θεώρημα) and as a likeness (εἰκών) of something absent; how the soul recognises the present image as a likeness of the absent thing without already possessing access to the absent thing constitutes, as noted in the conceptual tensions, a representational puzzle at the heart of Aristotle's philosophy of mind. Caston emphasises that phantasia can be false: Aristotle holds that "a scene-painting or a dream are both 'something, but not what they produce a phantasia of'" (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). This capacity for falsehood distinguishes the phantasma sharply from veridical perception and reveals why thinking cannot be a mere bodily process; for the materialist account, grounded in the principle that like is known by like, cannot the soul errs. The voluntariness of phantasia—our ability, at the deliberative grade, to summon and manipulate images at will—further separates it from the passivity of aisthesis and will receive sustained treatment in the discussion of deliberative phantasia below. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme The relationship between φαντασία and μνήμη (memory) further illuminates the distance Aristotle places between his own cognitive psychology and the materialist reduction of thought to perception. Memory, for Aristotle, requires that a previously perceived object be re-presented to the soul in its absence; thus memory depends upon the phantasma as its sensory residue, yet it adds a temporal determination that phantasia as such does not possess—namely, the recognition that the image pertains to something past. Kevin White observes that Aristotle's treatment of phantasia in *De Anima* III.3–8 follows a systematic plan in which "first the essence of the soul, and then the properties of which the essence is the cause, are to be treated in turn" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 6). Within this architectonic, phantasia occupies a position between perception and the higher cognitive powers precisely because it furnishes the material upon which memory and thought subsequently operate. Phantasia contrasts with memory insofar as the image produced by phantasia need not carry the retrospective index that memory demands; one may entertain a phantasma of warmth without thereby remembering a particular fire. Yet without phantasia's prior generation of images, memory would have no content to temporally mark as past. The materialist who collapses all cognition into bodily affection cannot account for this layered structure, for perception alone grasps only the present object; it is phantasia that preserves the sensory trace and thereby makes possible both voluntary recall and involuntary reminiscence. As Christina Papachristou notes, the Greek word "phantasia" resists translation as mere "imagination," since it encompasses a range of psychic functions—sensory, mnemonic, deliberative—that no single English term captures (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). The relation of phantasia to doxa (belief) and its role in the grades of sensitive versus deliberative phantasia will be addressed in the section that follows. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The distinction between φαντασία and δόξα (belief or opinion) constitutes one of Aristotle's most decisive interventions against the materialist conflation of thinking with perceiving. If all thinking were a bodily process like perceiving, then there would be no principled difference between having an appearance and holding a belief; yet Aristotle insists that phantasia and doxa diverge in several respects. White reports that Aristotle's second indication distinguishing phantasia from thinking is that "genuine fearful judgment immediately moves us emotionally, whereas phantasia" may present a fearful scene without producing the corresponding affective response—one may entertain the image of danger as one might contemplate "a painting" without experiencing genuine terror (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, p. 6). This asymmetry reveals that phantasia does not entail conviction (πίστις), whereas doxa necessarily involves commitment to the truth or falsity of its content; accordingly, phantasia explains doxa by furnishing the representational material upon which belief subsequently operates, without being itself a species of belief. Heidegger's reading of Aristotle corroborates this interpretive trajectory, for he emphasises that rhetoric's aim is κρίσις—"a definite decision in the sense of a δόξα"—achieved through discourse that brings hearers "into a corresponding frame of mind" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 124). The construction of such a frame of mind presupposes the operation of phantasia, which renders objects present to the soul in their affective salience, thus mediating between the sheer givenness of perceptual appearance and the evaluative posture of opinion. Caston's analysis reinforces this point: because phantasia can be false in a manner distinct from perceptual error, and because Aristotle holds that false appearances do not automatically produce false beliefs, the image-making faculty occupies an autonomous stratum within the soul's cognitive economy (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 15–16). Thus Aristotle's critique of the ancients depends fundamentally upon his theory of phantasia, for it is only by recognising phantasia as a capacity that is neither perception nor belief, yet mediates between both, that one can explain error, temporal cognition, and the voluntary manipulation of images—phenomena that the materialist equation of thought with bodily process cannot accommodate.
